# The Kilogram That Couldn't Be Wrong

For 130 years, the kilogram was a particular object. It sat in a vault in Sèvres, just outside Paris: a cylinder of platinum-iridium alloy about as tall as a golf ball, kept under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault required three keys held by three different people. The object was called the International Prototype Kilogram, or Le Grand K, and it did not weigh a kilogram the way a bag of sugar does. It was the kilogram. Whatever it weighed, that was the answer.

I find this arrangement endlessly interesting, mostly because of the logical corner it painted everyone into.

When the prototype was made in the 1880s, a batch of near-identical copies was cast alongside it and distributed to national laboratories around the world. Every few decades, some of those copies travelled back to Sèvres to be compared against the original. This happened in 1889, in 1946, and again around 1990. By the third comparison a pattern had emerged: the copies and the prototype were drifting apart. On average, the copies had gained about 50 micrograms relative to the original over a century, roughly the mass of a small grain of sand.

Nobody could say which side had changed. Perhaps the copies were picking up contaminants from the air. Perhaps the prototype was losing something, such as hydrogen slowly escaping the alloy. The measurements could only show a difference, and the definition made the question stranger still, because the prototype could not change by definition. If it shed a few atoms, then officially it still weighed exactly one kilogram, and everything else in the universe had become slightly heavier. That sounds like a joke, but it is simply what follows from defining a unit as a thing.

The French revolutionaries who invented the metric system had wanted to avoid exactly this. Their ambition was a system of measurement taken from nature rather than from a king's forearm or a local merchant's bushel. The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. The kilogram would be the mass of a litre of water. The motto was "for all time, for all people": no one would own the units, and anyone could in principle reconstruct them.

To get the metre, two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years in the 1790s surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona by triangulation, through a revolution and a war, getting arrested as spies along the way. Méchain found a discrepancy of a few arcseconds in his Barcelona latitude measurements that he could not explain. He concealed it, agonized over it for the rest of his life, and died of yellow fever in Spain while trying to extend the survey and redeem himself. The metre that came out of the project was about a fifth of a millimetre short of its own definition, though mostly for reasons other than his error.

After all that, practicality won. You can't resurvey France every time you need to calibrate a ruler, so a platinum bar was made to embody the result, and a platinum cylinder to embody the litre of water, and those became the legal standards. Nature provided the justification, but the metal was the law. By 1889, when the international prototypes were installed at Sèvres, the pretense was dropped entirely, and the metre and kilogram were defined as those objects.

The twentieth century slowly returned to the original dream, with better tools. In 1960 the metre was redefined in terms of wavelengths of light from krypton atoms, and in 1983 as the distance light travels in a specified fraction of a second. The second itself became a count of oscillations in caesium atoms. One by one the units were detached from artifacts and tied to things that are the same everywhere.

The kilogram held out longest, because mass is hard. Two approaches eventually got good enough. One involved making nearly perfect spheres of ultra-pure silicon, among the roundest objects ever manufactured, and effectively counting the atoms in them. The other was the Kibble balance, a machine that weighs an object against an electromagnetic force and measures that force through quantum electrical effects, linking mass to the Planck constant. It is named for Bryan Kibble, the British physicist who conceived it and who died in 2016, two years before it changed the definition.

In November 2018, delegates from member nations met at Versailles and voted unanimously to redefine the kilogram. The change took effect on 20 May 2019. The new definition does not mention any object. It fixes the numerical value of the Planck constant, exactly, and lets the kilogram be whatever makes that value come out right.

What I enjoy most is the inversion this performed. Before 2019, the Planck constant was a measured quantity with experimental uncertainty, and the cylinder in Sèvres had a mass of exactly one kilogram with no uncertainty at all. Afterwards, the Planck constant became exact by decree, and the cylinder became an ordinary object whose mass has to be measured, with error bars like anything else. For the first time since 1889, Le Grand K is allowed to be wrong.

The other thing I enjoy is that the whole enterprise was engineered so that no one would notice. Decades of work by hundreds of people across competing national laboratories, pushing measurements to a few parts in a hundred million, and success was defined as continuity: your bathroom scale, your pharmacy, and your grocery store all carried on exactly as before. Metrology may be the only field where the goal of a revolution is that nothing changes.

The revolutionary motto is only half fulfilled, though. In principle, anyone anywhere can now realize the kilogram from scratch. In practice, a Kibble balance costs millions and only a handful exist, so most of the world still gets its kilogram through a chain of metal weights compared against other metal weights, ending at a lab that has one. The definition belongs to everyone, but the equipment doesn't yet.

The cylinder itself is still in the vault, under its three bell jars. The metrologists intend to keep weighing it from time to time. After a century of being unable to ask the question, they would like to find out which way it was drifting.

I need to pick a topic for a 1000-word piece, something specific and not generic, the kind of thing I'd actually find interesting to write about, and avoid the usual autopilot phrasing.

I'm weighing a couple of more concrete options now, like river meanders, where a 1996 claim that their curves approach pi has since looked shakier in later data. The kilogram idea appeals too: a platinum-iridium cylinder in Sèvres that drifted against its copies by roughly 50 micrograms over a century before the unit was redefined.

I'm settling on the kilogram as the subject: the old platinum cylinder couldn't have drifted, since it defined the unit, so the rest of the world must have gotten heavier. Then the 2019 switch to fixing the Planck constant, the Kibble balance, and the silicon spheres for the Avogadro project come to mind, along with the earlier metre and second definitions and Méchain's concealed surveying error.

I'm checking the historical facts now: the cleaning routine for the platinum cylinder, the three keys needed to open its vault, and the handful of times it was taken out for comparison, starting with 1889 and running through 2014. I'm also starting to work through how the divergence from its copies was measured.

I'm going over the kilogram's drift: the platinum cylinder's copies had gained about 50 micrograms against it over a century, roughly the weight of a small grain of sand. Then I'm turning to the Kibble balance, which weighs a mass against an electromagnetic force and ties the result to the Planck constant through quantum effects. That meant the machine measured the constant before 2019, and afterward the constant was fixed so the same machine could realize the kilogram; the change was voted unanimously in Versailles in November 2018 and took effect that May.

I'm recalling Méchain's survey from Rodez to Barcelona, where he found a discrepancy of about three arcseconds in the latitude readings and kept it to himself. He died of yellow fever in Spain in 1804 while trying to extend the work. The meter that came out of it ended up roughly 0.2 mm short of its intended length, mostly from a wrong assumption about the Earth's flattening rather than his concealed error. I'm also noting that the 1799 platinum kilogram was defined as the mass of a litre of water at 4°C, which is a different basis from the original 1795 gram.

Now I'm picturing the kilogram as an object in a vault, a platinum-iridium cylinder roughly the height of a golf ball, kept under three glass bell jars and opened only with three separate keys held by three people. It was called Le Grand K, and it wasn't a weight measured against something else; it simply defined what a kilogram was.

I'm turning to the drift itself: the copies had gained roughly 50 micrograms against the original over a century, and nobody could say which side had changed. The prototype might have been shedding something or the copies might have been picking up contaminants, but by definition the prototype could not be the one that moved, so the mismatch pointed at everything else.

Now I'm weighing the inversion: the platinum prototype was the standard, so the rest of the world would have had to be the thing that changed. From there I'm turning to the revolutionaries' original plan of anchoring units to nature, with the metre from the Earth and the kilogram from water, and how Méchain's concealed survey error shadows that story. The practical retreat to platinum bars followed, since nobody could re-survey a meridian every time a ruler needed calibrating.

I'm picturing the kilogram's drift as a kind of quiet embarrassment: the cylinder is the yardstick, so if anything has moved, it must be everything else. Then I'm weighing the second half of the idea, that the 2019 redefinition was built so nobody would notice the change, and that the whole achievement rests on continuity. I'm also turning over the "for all people" promise: in principle anyone with a good enough lab can realize the kilogram, but a Kibble balance costs millions and only a handful exist, so most of the world still inherits its kilogram through a chain of metal objects compared against other metal objects.

I'm settling on the last beat of the piece: the cylinder stays under its bell jars, and metrologists still plan to weigh it, hoping to finally learn which way it drifted. I'll close with that and keep to roughly a thousand words.
